# "Superhuman" Robots in Teams: The Effect of Augmented Cognitive Capabilities on Human-Robot Communication

## Abstract

As social robots become increasingly advanced, the rules of human-robot interaction (HRI) may diverge from those of interpersonal communication. In this light, scholars have proposed that the Computers-Are-Social-Actors (CASA) paradigm, which proposes that we respond to machines as we do with humans, may need to be revised. The aim of this study was to investigate whether original CASA findings on interdependence in human-computer interaction hold in interactions with an advanced (i.e., augmented) social robot. To this end, we conducted a 2 (display of augmented cognitive capabilities: control vs. augmented) x 2 (interdependency: interdependent vs. non-interdependent) between-subjects experiment with 260 participants. We measured behavioral conformity, entitativity, and interactivity as outcomes. Interdependency did not have any effect on any of the variables. However, augmentation increased behavioral conformity. These results present tentative evidence that further research on CASA is warranted and suggest the need for a comprehensive theoretical framework to account for technological advancements and explain interactions with advanced media agents.

While the CASA framework has been widely supported [7, 8] , recent research has criticized it for being somewhat outdated [9, 10] and showing an "anthropocentric bias" (e.g., [9] ). Specifically, this anthropocentric bias refers to the importance placed on an exclusively human-centered point-of-view along with an understanding of communication as derived from human-human communication only [11, 12] . In this context, Gambino et al. [9] have pointed out that research in the CASA framework largely focuses on "what makes media agents human, rather than what makes them special" ( [13] , p. 494, as quoted in [9] ).

The anthropocentric bias seems particularly problematic in the context of human-robot interaction (HRI), which may resemble, but also differs considerably from, interpersonal interactions (e.g., [14] ). While social robots are similar to humans in that they are created specifically to interact socially with humans [15] , their abilities may, in some respects, supersede those of humans [10] . When media agents present humanlike social attri butes (e.g., human voices), users will thus perceive these agents as autonomous social actors, leading to an activa tion of social scripts. The CASA framework, specifically, proposes that these social scripts are mindlessly activated in interactions with machines after repeated and continuous exposure to social cues in human-human communication [19]. The social scripts learned in human-human communi cation are thus automatically (i.e., mindlessly) applied also to media agents [20]. CASA has been supported by several studies, including multiple experiments conducted by Nass and colleagues from the late 1990s onwards [7]. These experimental stud ies demonstrated that social responses towards computers were easy to generate: Among others, people applied gen der stereotypes to computers [21]; exhibited polite behav ior toward them [22]; responded differently to computers equipped with different voices [21]; and preferred comput ers that flattered them [21]. More recently, similar findings have been obtained in HMC research focusing on different interfaces (e.g., embodied conversational agents [23, 24]; mobile phones [25]). Looking specifically at social robots, empirical replications of original CASA studies found, for example, that male- rather than female-gendered robots were preferred as security guards [26], and that people are more likely to help robots that are familiar, perceived as peers, and make smaller requests [27]. However, several scholars have also questioned CASA’s claims (e.g., [9, 28]), both theoretically and empirically. At a theoretical level, scholars have criticized the conceptual underpinnings of CASA (e.g., [29]). In proposing the Media are Social Actors (MASA) paradigm as a more refined and structured extension of CASA, Lombard and Xu [10], for example, maintain that explicit propositions that could be examined, tested, and refined are missing in CASA. Simi larly, Gambino and colleagues [9] have argued that the idea that people apply human-human interaction scripts to inter actions with media agents is outdated for three key reasons. First, people’s increased knowledge and experience with media agents have resulted in the development of special ized scripts for interactions with media agents. Second, technological advancements have made media agents more humanlike, reducing the mindlessness of social responses toward them. Third and finally, interactions between media agents and people have changed due to agents’ increased social affordances (i.e., abilities to accommodate the user’s communication [30]), personalization, and bandwidth of communicative (social) cues [9]. At an empirical level, and in line with these critiques, multiple studies on different forms of HMC have obtained findings that are incompatible with the predictions of the CASA paradigm. For instance, Lang et al. [28] failed to fully replicate the application of politeness norms to com puters and suggested that computers are no longer perceived as well-defined physical partners to which politeness norms, and social norms more generally, apply [28]. In addition, Bastiansen and colleagues [31] demonstrated that gender cues did not elicit stereotypical social responses toward a chatbot, and a recent study by Liu et al. [32] found no effect of assigned names (i.e., identity cues) on self-disclosure toward chatbots. In a direct replication of the politeness study [22], Hey selaar [33] also found no difference in the evaluation of a computer when being interviewed by the same or a different computer. Heyselaar [33] highlights that the lack of polite ness of people to computers in her investigation may indicate a novelty effect in the original study, in which people with less exposure to technology exhibited a social-desirability effect in being polite to computers. ## Introduction

With autonomous machines pervading various sectors of everyday life, ranging from healthcare [1, 2] to education [3, 4] , machines are no longer just a medium of communication but also participants in communicative interactions [5] . As such interactions become increasingly ubiquitous, it is essential to have a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms of human-machine communication (HMC). An important framework that has widely been used to explain these mechanisms is the Computers-Are-Social-Actors (CASA) framework [6] . CASA proposes that humans see media agents (e.g., computers, mobile phones, of data in real-time [16] . Such AI skills may be considered augmented versions of 'human' skills (e.g., information processing, logical reasoning). However, the ubiquity of the anthropocentric bias in our understanding of communication with media agents has led to such 'superhuman' elements of social robots being underrepresented in HRI research [10] .

In the present study, we responded to this critique by investigating whether 'special' skills of social robots challenge the anthropocentric bias and, by extension, the equation of media agents with humans. To this end, we conceptually replicated and extended a study by Nass et al. [17] on the applicability of the interdependency social script in human-computer teams. More specifically, we conducted an experimental study to investigate the impact of a social robot's display of augmented cognitive capabilities on human-robot team behavior (e.g., perceiving the robot as a team member and conforming to the robot's decisions). If our findings mirror those presented by Nass et al. [17] , this provides further evidence for the robustness of the CASA paradigm. If not, our findings present tentative evidence of an anthropocentric bias that may call for rethinking the CASA framework in the light of recent technological developments.

## Theoretical Background

The CASA framework was inspired by Reeves and Nass' [18] The Media Equation, which posits that the human brain has not evolved to distinguish between media and real-world agents. When media agents present humanlike social attributes (e.g., human voices), users will thus perceive these agents as autonomous social actors, leading to an activation of social scripts. The CASA framework, specifically, proposes that these social scripts are mindlessly activated in interactions with machines after repeated and continuous exposure to social cues in human-human communication [19] . The social scripts learned in human-human communication are thus automatically (i.e., mindlessly) applied also to media agents [20] .

CASA has been supported by several studies, including multiple experiments conducted by Nass and colleagues from the late 1990s onwards [7] . These experimental studies demonstrated that social responses towards computers were easy to generate: Among others, people applied gender stereotypes to computers [21] ; exhibited polite behavior toward them [22] ; responded differently to computers equipped with different voices [21] ; and preferred computers that flattered them [21] . More recently, similar findings have been obtained in HMC research focusing on different interfaces (e.g., embodied conversational agents [23, 24] ; mobile phones [25] ). Looking specifically at social robots, empirical replications of original CASA studies found, for example, that male-rather than female-gendered robots were preferred as security guards [26] , and that people are more likely to help robots that are familiar, perceived as peers, and make smaller requests [27] .

However, several scholars have also questioned CASA's claims (e.g., [9, 28] ), both theoretically and empirically. At a theoretical level, scholars have criticized the conceptual underpinnings of CASA (e.g., [29] ). Similarly, Gambino and colleagues [9] have argued that the idea that people apply human-human interaction scripts to interactions with media agents is outdated for three key reasons.
